bib.title: Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning

question: Which weight-update rules for networks of stochastic units move, on average, along the gradient of expected reinforcement without computing or storing a gradient estimate?
contributions: Define the REINFORCE class (nonnegative rate x offset reinforcement x characteristic eligibility) and prove (Theorem 1) that its mean update has nonnegative inner product with the gradient of E{r|W}
Extend to episodic tasks via unfolding in time (Theorem 2)
Show existing algorithms (L_R-I, A_R-I) are REINFORCE algorithms and derive new ones (Gaussian units, multiparameter distributions; Proposition 1)
Show how REINFORCE combines with backpropagation through deterministic units and through random number generators

results.claim: The reinforcement baseline in REINFORCE may be an adaptive estimate of upcoming reinforcement (reinforcement comparison) as long as it is never computed from the current y_i or current r.
results.setup: Bernoulli-logistic units, rule dw_ij = alpha (r - rbar)(y_i - p_i) x_j, rbar updated by exponential averaging rbar(t)=gamma r(t-1)+(1-gamma) rbar(t-1), 0<gamma<=1 (Eqs 9-10).
results.quote: the use of reinforcement comparison (Sutton, 1984) is also consistent with the REINFORCE for- mulation.

results.claim: The theory gives no basis for choosing among baselines (no variance result); the preference for reinforcement comparison is empirical.
results.setup: Statement about the analysis, applying to all REINFORCE baselines.
results.quote: While the analytical results given here offer no basis for comparing various choices of reinforcement baseline in REINFORCE algorithms, it is generally believed that the use of reinforcement comparison leads to algorithms having superior performance in general.

results.claim: Extensive empirical experience shows an adaptive baseline can greatly speed convergence and change qualitative behavior, though Theorem 1 applies to any baseline.
results.setup: Informal summary of simulation experience (Sutton 1984, Williams and Peng 1991, Gaussian unit studies); no numbers or protocol given.
results.quote: extensive empirical investigation of such algorithms leads to the inescapable conclusion that use of an adaptive reinforcement baseline incorporating something like the reinforcement comparison strategy can greatly
results.note: Continues: 'emhance convergence speed, and, in some cases, can lead to a big difference in qualitative behavior as well.'

results.claim: With b = 0 and always-positive r, a single Bernoulli unit performs a biased random walk with nonzero probability of converging to the inferior output; any baseline lying between the two reward values gives motion always toward the better output.
results.setup: Single Bernoulli semilinear unit with only a bias weight, output y affecting r deterministically.
results.quote: If r is always positive, it is easy to see that one obtains a kind of biased random walk behavior when b = 0, leading to nonzero probability of convergence to the inferior output value.
results.note: The paper also says the second behavior (motion always toward the better output) occurs for any b lying between the two possible values of r.

results.claim: The variance-minimising baseline is not the mean reinforcement; Dayan (1990) found at most a slight convergence-speed gain over mean reinforcement.
results.setup: Nonassociative simulations as summarised by Williams; no numbers given.
results.quote: This turns out to yield not the mean reinforcement as in the usual reinforcement comparison approach, but another quantity that is more difficult to estimate effectively.
results.note: The words 'minimizes the variance of the individual weight changes over time' are on the preceding line. The paper does not prove any variance-reduction claim itself.

results.claim: In Sutton (1984) single-Bernoulli-unit studies, REINFORCE with reinforcement comparison outperformed all other algorithms investigated.
results.setup: Nonassociative and associative immediate-reinforcement tasks, single Bernoulli unit, no numbers given.
results.quote: REINFORCE with reinforcement comparison was found to outperform all other algorithms investigated.

results.claim: Expected motion is toward the best action, yet L_R-I converges to an inferior action with nonzero probability, so Theorem 1 does not give convergence.
results.setup: 2-action L_R-I automaton, compared to a biased random walk with absorbing barriers.
results.quote: there is always a nonzero probability of its converging to an inferior choice of action.

results.claim: A_R-I and L_R-I are REINFORCE algorithms with b=0; the Bernoulli-logistic eligibility is (y_i - p_i) x_j, giving dw_ij = alpha r (y_i - p_i) x_j.
results.setup: Network of Bernoulli-logistic units, b_ij = 0, alpha_ij = alpha (Eqs 7-8).
results.quote: Thus AR-b when applied to a network of Bernoulli-logistic units, is a REINFORCE algorithm.

results.claim: Proposition 1: for exponential-family densities with mean mu, d ln g / d mu = (y - mu)/sigma^2, covering Bernoulli, normal, Poisson, exponential.
results.setup: g = exp[Q y + D + S(y)] with mu the mean; proof in Appendix B.
results.quote: the characteristic eligibility of the mean parameter has this form for an even wider variety of distributions

results.claim: Without a baseline, a Gaussian unit with nonnegative r may drive sigma to 0 before mu reaches a hill top.
results.setup: Nonassociative single-variable function optimization, Gaussian unit with adaptable mu and sigma; simulation details not given.
results.quote: REINFORCE may cause a to converge to 0 before/z has moved to the top of any hill.
results.note: 'a' is OCR for sigma; 'if r is always nonnegative and reinforcement comparison is not used (i.e., b = 0)'.

limits: No asymptotic or convergence theory: 'The main disadvantages are the lack of a general convergence theory applicable to this class of algorithms and, as with all gradient algorithms, an apparent susceptibility to convergence to false optima.'
Theorems only cover the expected update direction; they say nothing about variance, so no basis for choosing a baseline (Section 4 and 8.3).
Assumes stationary, independent input and reward distributions; immediate reinforcement, with only an episodic extension that spreads credit uniformly over time steps (found especially slow).
Simulation evidence is cited from other work or called preliminary; no numbers, hyperparameters, seeds or datasets reported.
REINFORCE is generally very slow even when it succeeds.

terms.definition: Update dw_ij = alpha_ij (r - b_ij) e_ij with alpha_ij nonnegative and dependent at most on w_i and t, baseline b_ij conditionally independent of y_i given W and x_i, e_ij = d ln g_i / d w_ij. Name is an acronym for 'REward Increment = Nonnegative Factor x Offset Reinforcement x Characteristic Eligibility'.
e_ij = d ln g_i / d w_ij, the log-derivative of the unit's output probability mass or density with respect to the weight.
Maintaining an adaptive estimate of upcoming reinforcement from past experience and using it as the baseline b.
